---
title: "Thesis kit: From item responses to a Methods section"
description: >
  A step-by-step path for a thesis or dissertation that uses IRT: Check the
  data, choose and check a model, make the figures, and draft the Methods
  paragraph with cite_methods().
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      warning = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
                      out.width = "100%", dpi = 96)
```

A thesis committee wants three things from an IRT analysis: That the model
was chosen for a reason, that it was checked, and that the write-up says
exactly what was done. This kit walks through all three with one dataset,
and ends with a Methods paragraph and reference list you can paste into
your thesis and then edit.

The example uses `SAT12`, a 32-item science test taken by 600 students,
which comes with mirt. Swap in your own data at step 1 and run the rest as
it is.

## The checklist

Keep this list next to your draft. Each step below covers one line.

- [ ] Describe the data and run a classical item analysis.
- [ ] Compare at least two IRT models and say why you chose one.
- [ ] Check dimensionality, local independence and item fit.
- [ ] Report overall fit (M2 or C2 with RMSEA, SRMSR and CFI) and reliability.
- [ ] Make the figures: A Wright map and test information at minimum.
- [ ] Write the Methods paragraph and cite mirt and mirtverse.
- [ ] Save the code and an HTML report as an appendix.

## 1. Describe the data

```{r data}
library(mirtverse)

key <- c(1,4,5,2,3,1,2,1,3,1,2,4,2,1,5,3,4,4,1,4,3,3,4,1,3,5,1,3,1,5,4,5)
data <- key2binary(SAT12, key)       # score multiple-choice answers 0/1
dim(data)
```

```{r itemstats}
head(itemstats(data)$itemstats)       # classical item statistics
```

Look for items that almost everyone gets right or wrong, and for items with
a low or negative item-total correlation: They are often miskeyed. If you
remove an item, write down why; `cite_methods()` can report it (step 5).

## 2. Choose a model

`select_model()` fits the candidate models to the same data, compares them,
and explains its choice in plain language. Quote that reasoning in your
thesis rather than just the winner.

```{r select}
sel <- select_model(data, candidates = c("Rasch", "2PL"), verbose = FALSE)
sel
mod <- sel$best
```

## 3. Check the model

Three checks most committees ask about: Overall fit, item fit and local
dependence.

```{r glance}
glance(mod)[, c("M2", "df", "p.value", "RMSEA", "SRMSR", "CFI", "reliability")]
```

```{r itemfit}
gg_itemfit(mod)
```

```{r q3}
gg_q3(mod)
```

`interpret(mod)` writes a plain-language summary of these results, which is
a good check on your own reading of them.

## 4. Make the figures

Every plot is a ggplot2 object. Save figures at the size of your page, at
300 dpi, so the text in them matches the text around them.

```{r wright, fig.height = 5}
p <- gg_wright(mod)
p
```

```{r info}
gg_info(mod)
```

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
ggplot2::ggsave("figure-1-wright-map.png", p, width = 6.5, height = 4.5, dpi = 300)
```

For an item-by-item table in the results chapter, `item_table(mod)` has
the item statistics, fit and flags in one data frame. Write it to a CSV
file and paste it into Word as a table:

```{r table, eval = FALSE}
write.csv(item_table(mod), "table-2-items.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

## 5. Write the Methods paragraph

`cite_methods()` drafts the software, model, estimation, model choice, fit
and reliability sentences, in APA style, with the references they cite.
Give it the `select_model()` result so it describes the comparison too.

```{r methods}
cite_methods(sel, sample = "high school students",
             items = "multiple-choice science items")
```

To get a Word file with the paragraph and the references:

```{r docx, eval = FALSE}
cite_methods(sel, sample = "high school students",
             items = "multiple-choice science items",
             file = "methods.docx")
```

Treat the text as a first draft. Read it against your analysis, add what
only you know (how the data were collected, ethics approval, why the test
was given), and rewrite it in your own voice. Your committee will read it
as yours.

## 6. Keep an appendix

One HTML file holds the whole analysis: Model comparison, parameters,
fit, figures and item health cards.

```{r report, eval = FALSE}
mv_report(sel, file = "appendix-irt-analysis.html")
```

Save your R script next to it. If someone asks how a number was produced,
the script answers.
